why: It gives the area as the castle's own, but its round 50 ha matches the present national historic site and park (about 49.2 ha by the park's own page), so it is a modern measure of the grounds that survive inside the outer moats, not a survey of the period; the castle town and the retainers' quarters outside them are not in it, and it is one castle of a northern domain of 100,000 koku, an example rather than a rule. It does not say whether the moats are counted.

It says the park opens nearly the whole of the domain's castle and that the castle's layout as first built survives entire, which makes today's area the Edo castle's. It gives two areas that disagree, about 49 ha in its text and 385,200 square meters in its overview, and says neither what each counts nor why they differ. And they are one northern domain's castle, not a size for castles in general.

It states the water soak, the unhairing with lime or urine, the bating with dog or pigeon dung, the salt curing of raw hides and the trade's place at the outskirts, which are the process and the siting this page's tanning yard draws. General and largely Western history; it says nothing of Japan.

It dates the Suitengu faith before the modern period: the lords of Kurume revered the shrine for its powers against water disasters and for safe birth and in 1818 enshrined it at their Edo residence, where its faith spread to the neighbors. The one entry that calls the shrine a guardian of boats says so in the present tense with no date; the entries also differ on what was set up in Edo in 1818, a place to worship from afar or the enshrined god itself.

It gives a domain's own lot for its lowest samurai, settled on the moors by about 1609, larger than the lower lots of Fukui's table, with half of it a vegetable field. It clashes with itself on two figures (some 6,000 retainers moved, yet some 8,000 became harakata-shu; a lot of 150 tsubo, yet a frontage of 6 to 8 ken by a depth of about 25 ken, which makes 150 to 200), the article does not date the lot rule, and the depth is cited to a note on a 1769 map of the harakata residences, so the figures may record the lots as they stood a century and a half on rather than as first granted; any moor a household cleared beyond its lot became its own, so a holding could be larger than the lot; and these were half-farming samurai on the town's edge, not a castle town's ordinary ward.
It describes the chambered tunnel climbing a slope with its firebox low and its chimney high, which is the kiln form these maps draw.

A Shin historian's article in a standard encyclopedia that dates the Shin priest's wife from dated documents: a list of 1343 naming the wife of the head of a dōjō, and Rennyo's fifteenth-century letters on the wives of the priests of the lodging houses. Its limits: we read the article, not the documents it cites; the 1343 instance is the wife of the head of a dōjō, a meeting hall, not of a temple; it attests the wife and her role in running temples and dōjō, not the rest of the household, and says nothing of where the household lived or of other sects.

It places a shrine's hereditary priest families (社家) in a quarter of their own, a short walk from the shrine along the priests' path, which it says lasted until the Meiji era (it gives no year). Its limits: it gives no date for the quarter's beginning, no count of houses and no plan, and it concerns a shrine's priests, not a temple's.

It dates to the Edo period an old monk's own residence standing apart from the monastery, in the town below it. Its limits: it concerns celibate monks of one great monastery, not families, and gives no count or size.

It says the ground round the temple was lined with priests' quarters and lodgings for believers and formed a temple town, which places the clergy's houses round a temple in fifteenth-century Japan. Its limits: its sentence on the temple town has no footnote (the article's only printed reference is a 2018 popular book about prefectural borders); Yoshizaki was the seat of the sect's head and a pilgrimage center, not an ordinary temple; it gives no count, size or plan of the houses.

It is a drill hall built and dated before 1912, and gives its width in bays and its south-facing, hip-and-gable form. It is an imperial camp's hall at the capital, not a county's, so it shows what a large state drill hall could be rather than a county's; it gives bays, not meters, and describes the hall as it stands after its 1988-2003 repairs (from Beijing gazetteers of 2004-2006), not from a Qing record; a Beijing government page dates the hall to 1749, a year later than the article.

The Yamakawa entry, a reference work by historians, says the Edo-period chugen lived together in large rooms in their lord's residence. It names the room (the chugen room, one of the large rooms) but gives no plan, no size and no count of the men in a room; its only number is the shogunate's own 540-560 chugen. It speaks of the residences of the domain lords (藩邸), not of a country office.

It describes the traditional charcoal burn as a hemispherical pile sealed with earth, which is the low mound shape this page contrasts with the potter's tunnel kiln. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. And the article is European throughout, German in its terms and examples; the earth-covered pile is a form East Asia also knew, but the page does not say so.

It dates a barracks whose squad rooms are furnished with wooden beds to the first years of the modern army, the earliest barracks with beds found. The wooden beds are a display that recreates the rooms "as they were at the time" without saying what time. The building was in use until 1963, so 1873 is the date of the building, not of its beds. The page does not say when beds first came into a Japanese barracks. The building was also cut to about 70% of its length and is shown with windows added after it was built, so its plan is not the 1873 form.
It dates the manual to 1149 and names its subject as the wet-rice farming of the Jiangnan region, the lower Yangtze, which is all it is used for. It names no sources of its own.

It reads the shigarami of an 8th-century poem as stakes driven in with wood or bamboo laid across to dam the water, and likens it to the weir excavated at the Kodera site, tying the word to a built form. It is a column without footnotes; the build and the Kodera likeness are the column's own reading, not what the poem says, and it gives no size and says nothing about China.

It gives the firing's length and its round-the-clock stoking, which is why this page keeps the potters living at the kiln, and the sloped tunnel form the kiln glyph draws. It does not name the noborigama. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. Its account of the firing blends historic Asian kilns with modern studio practice, so the days-long firing is a modern potter's as much as a premodern one's.
It dates the collection's poems to the 11th to 7th centuries BC, which places a poem of it far before modern times. It does not date the commentaries printed with the poems.
It dates the compilation to about 239 BC, which places the text's rule on burial far before modern times.

It states that the kiln city stood at its clay and that its imperial kilns sat at the city's center with the others four kilometers out, which is the kiln-at-the-clay siting this page follows. Its one passage on where the workers lived describes seasonal migrants in sheds in 1905, not resident kiln households. The page gives no period for the arrangement of the imperial kilns at the center and the others four kilometers out, and Jingdezhen is the exceptional case - a national industry grown into a city - standing behind a county seat's single works.

It dates the manual (1680-1682 in the Nipponica entry, the Tenna years 1681-1684 in Heibonsha's, 1673-1684 in Yamakawa's), which is what places what the manual says before 1868. Its limits: it summarizes the manual rather than quoting it. Each date is the editors' estimate, not a year the manual gives: the manual names no author and no year of writing, and it survived only in manuscript copies (Nipponica). So the three ranges differ, but all fall between 1673 and 1684, well before 1868. The manual describes farming in Mikawa and Totomi (today's Aichi and Shizuoka), one region of Japan, not the whole country.
It gives the firing range that sets fine stoneware apart from a county works' earthenware.

It dates the woods, not their size: many have stood for well over 300 years and some over 600, and much of Hong Kong's other forest is post-war regrowth, which tells a reader the surviving woods are not a modern planting. It gives no area for any wood, says nothing of whether a wood has grown or shrunk, and gives its ages without naming how they were found. Hong Kong is subtropical southern China, not Japan.
It shows the bamboo-grove symbol in use on the national survey's maps of about 1910, well after 1868. It does not say when the symbol was introduced, and it says nothing of maps before modern times.

It gives the firing range of the coarse ware a county works makes, beside the stoneware article's range for the finer body, which is the temperature gap this page argues from. The sentence carrying the firing range has no citation on the page.

It names the districts each known for one ware, which is this page's evidence that fine stoneware was a district's specialty rather than a county seat's. It does not say what an ordinary county seat did or did not fire. The grouping of six is a twentieth-century scholar's construct, devised after the war by Koyama Fujio; the districts are medieval, the canon is modern.

It is a prefectural seat's moat given in the old measure, over ten zhang wide, the size of moat the greater end of the band describes; but Zhengding was no common prefectural seat - a circuit of twenty-four li from 1449, triple gates the article calls rare in all the country, a city credited with guarding the capital - so its moat is a great seat's, not an ordinary one's. Its moat sentence carries no footnote and names no period or survey, so although the unit suggests an older record the figure cannot be dated; the article's one gazetteer footnote, to a county gazetteer published in 2008, is on its history section, not on the moat. The article also records the wall largely pulled down from 1958 and the moat (the Zhouhan River) put under a comprehensive rehabilitation from 2013, so the undated figure may describe the moat as it is now, not as the Ming or Qing dug it.

It states that the frame's old use was shoeing oxen, that it carries a belly sling, and that in Spain it was a village fixture, which is the standing frame this page's smithy apron carries. It gives no dimension. And the frame is a Western fixture: the page names England, Spain and America and no East Asian use, while Japan's own hoof practice was straw, so the frame on these maps is a transplant the smithy sentence labels as this page's reading.
